code.title: HashMap.put: hash spread, bucket index, return value

followUps:
It returns the previous value for that key, or null if the key was not there. The code replaces the value inside the existing node and hands back the old one. A null result is therefore ambiguous: the key may be absent, or it may have been mapped to null.

Example: put("a",1) returns null, then put("a",2) returns 1. Cost is the same O(1) average as the rest of put.

LinkedHashMap does not change put itself; it overrides three empty hook methods that HashMap calls at the end. HashMap.putVal calls newNode (LinkedHashMap creates an Entry and links it at the tail), then afterNodeAccess(e) when an existing key was updated (moves it to the tail in access-order mode), and afterNodeInsertion(evict) after a new key (asks removeEldestEntry and may drop the head).

That is how an LRU cache gets built from a plain HashMap flow at no extra asymptotic cost.

putIfAbsent stores the value only when the key is missing (or mapped to null) and returns the existing value otherwise. Internally it calls the same putVal with onlyIfAbsent = true, so the walk through the bucket is identical, but when an equal key is found the old value is kept instead of replaced.

Example: map has apple=5; putIfAbsent("apple",99) returns 5 and leaves 5; putIfAbsent("fig",3) returns null and inserts. In a plain HashMap it is not atomic across threads; ConcurrentHashMap makes it atomic.

code.title: Why a power-of-two table: mask equals modulo, spread folds high bits

followUps:
A prime-sized table spreads poorly chosen hashes better, but needs a real modulo and a full rehash on every resize. With prime n the index is h % n, a division (tens of cycles) and a sign fix for negatives; with 2^k it is one AND. On resize a prime table must recompute every index, while a power-of-two table only checks one bit (h & oldCap).

Java traded a little mixing quality for speed, then patched it with the spread step and treeification.

A strong hash costs far more per call than the table lookup it speeds up, and most keys do not need it. String, Integer and similar keys already have decent hashCodes; MurmurHash would add tens of nanoseconds to every get and put, which is slower than the occasional collision it prevents. Also the hashCode contract is the user's, and HashMap cannot re-hash a custom hash from inside.

The one XOR-shift costs about one cycle, and tree bins bound the damage of a bad hash to O(log n).

code.title: Treeification: colliding Comparable keys still found quickly

followUps:
The tree still works, but searching a bucket may have to scan it. If keys are not Comparable (or are different classes), the tree orders nodes by hash, then by System.identityHashCode/class name as a tie-break. With identical hashes that gives no useful order for a lookup, so find has to search both subtrees, which is O(k) for k colliding keys.

So treeification helps only Comparable keys; for others it is no worse than the list.

Every TreeNode extends the ordinary Node and keeps its next pointer, so iteration just walks the next chain. The tree structure (left, right, parent, red flag) is extra; insertion and removal keep the next links in a sensible order too. A for-each over the map therefore never needs to traverse the tree, only the same linked order a list bin would have.

Cost stays O(1) per element. The price is memory: a TreeNode is about twice the size of a Node.

code.title: Map implementations: null handling and compound actions

followUps:
When the code is simple, contention is low and you already have a Map you must make thread-safe. Examples: a small config map written once at start-up, a legacy API that needs a Map wrapper, or a map that is mostly used under one outer lock anyway. One mutex is fine when a few threads touch it a few times per second.

Also when you need null keys or values, which ConcurrentHashMap forbids. Remember to hold synchronized (map) yourself for compound actions and iteration.

Because the wrapper locks each method call, not the whole loop, so another thread can change the map between two iterator steps. The iterator checks modCount on every next(); if a writer thread inserts between your hasNext() and next(), the count differs and a ConcurrentModificationException is thrown.

Fix: wrap the whole loop in synchronized (map) { for (...) }, or copy the entries first, or use ConcurrentHashMap.

code.title: ConcurrentHashMap: atomic merge from many threads

followUps:
Because writers are changing the counters while size() reads them, so the sum may already be out of date when it returns. The map keeps baseCount plus striped CounterCells and size() adds them without stopping writers. If 4 threads each add 1 entry during the sum, the answer may miss some.

Treat it as an estimate for monitoring; use mappingCount() (returns long) for big maps, and never use size() to decide a correctness check like "is it empty so I can insert".

Negative hash values on a node mark special nodes that are not real entries. MOVED = -1 is a ForwardingNode meaning the bin has been moved to the new table during resize; TREEBIN = -2 is the wrapper for a red-black tree bin; RESERVED = -3 is a placeholder used by computeIfAbsent while it computes. Normal hashes are masked with HASH_BITS to stay non-negative, so no key can collide with these.

Because the bin stays locked while your function runs, so a slow function blocks every other thread using that bin. It also must not touch the same map: updating another key from inside can deadlock or throw IllegalStateException ("Recursive update") in Java 9+.

Example: a 200 ms database call inside computeIfAbsent stalls all keys hashing to the same bin. Keep it to cheap, pure work; for slow loads store a Future or use a cache library.

code.title: Why ConcurrentHashMap rejects null: get cannot tell absent from null

followUps:
Store a wrapper that says "not found" instead of null. Use Optional.empty(), or a shared sentinel object such as static final Object MISSING = new Object(), as the value. Then get returning null really means "never looked up", and a stored empty means "looked up, nothing there".

cache.computeIfAbsent(id, k -> Optional.ofNullable(db.find(k)));

Put a time limit on negative entries so a record added later is not hidden forever.

No, ConcurrentSkipListMap rejects null keys and null values too. Null keys fail because it must compare keys (a null cannot be compared); null values fail for the same "absent versus mapped to null" reason as ConcurrentHashMap. Both throw NullPointerException.

So the whole java.util.concurrent map family is null-free; only HashMap, LinkedHashMap and a few others permit nulls (and TreeMap allows null values but not null keys with natural ordering).

code.title: ArrayList growth: 1.5x capacities and total copies

followUps:
Because a fixed step makes the total work grow quadratically. If you add 10 slots each time, the copies for N adds are about N/10 resizes of average size N/2, i.e. N2/20 element copies. For N = 100,000 that is 500 million copies versus about 300,000 with 1.5x growth.

Geometric growth keeps the cost per add constant on average, at the price of up to 33% unused space.

remove(0) costs O(n) because every later element must slide one slot to the left. ArrayList calls System.arraycopy to shift elements [1..n-1] down to [0..n-2], then nulls the last slot. For 1,000,000 elements that is about 4 MB of memory moved per call.

Removing the last element is O(1). If you remove from the front often, use ArrayDeque (O(1) at both ends) or iterate once and rebuild.

Vector doubles its array by default. Its grow adds capacityIncrement if you set one, otherwise it adds the current capacity, so sizes go 10, 20, 40, 80. That wastes up to 50% of the array, versus ArrayList's 1.5x at about 33%. Every Vector method is also synchronized, which is why it is considered legacy.

code.title: ArrayList vs LinkedList: indexed access vs array shifting

followUps:
ArrayDeque stores elements in one array, so it does no allocation per element and keeps data together in memory. LinkedList creates a 24-byte Node for every offer, which costs allocation, garbage collection and a cache miss each time you follow a pointer. ArrayDeque only moves head and tail indexes in a circular buffer and doubles the array when full.

Both give O(1) at the ends; ArrayDeque is typically 2-5 times faster in benchmarks and it does not permit nulls.

About 4 bytes per element for ArrayList against about 24 bytes for LinkedList (plus the object itself in both). ArrayList holds one reference per slot (4 bytes with compressed oops, and up to 33% of slots may be unused). LinkedList allocates a Node: 12-byte header, item, next and prev (12 bytes) = 24 bytes after alignment.

For 1,000,000 Integers (16 bytes each): ~20 MB with ArrayList versus ~40 MB with LinkedList.

code.title: LRU cache using LinkedHashMap in access order

followUps:
Because get() in an LRU cache modifies the linked list, so it is a write and must not run in parallel with other gets. With a read lock, two threads can call get together and both relink the same nodes, corrupting before/after pointers or losing entries.

Use an exclusive lock (or synchronized) for every operation, or shard the cache into several independent LRUs, or use Caffeine, which records reads in a buffer and applies them later.

LRU evicts what was used longest ago, LFU evicts what is used least often, and W-TinyLFU combines both. LRU is simple but one big scan can flush every hot item. LFU keeps popular items but old favourites never leave. W-TinyLFU (used by Caffeine) puts new items in a small LRU window and admits them to the main area only if a compact frequency sketch says they are used more often than the victim.

Result: high hit rates with O(1) operations.

Store an expiry timestamp with each value and treat expired entries as missing. Wrap the value: record Entry(V v, long expiresAt). On get, if now > expiresAt remove it and return null; also check in removeEldestEntry or run a periodic cleanup so dead entries do not occupy slots.

Example: TTL 60 s, put at t=0, get at t=61 s returns a miss. Caffeine offers expireAfterWrite built in.

code.title: TreeMap: sorted navigation, comparator decides duplicates

followUps:
Take the smallest possible tree for a given black height and count its nodes. If every root-to-leaf path has b black nodes, the tree has at least 2b - 1 nodes, so b ≤ log2(n + 1). No red node has a red child, so red nodes can at most double a path: height h ≤ 2b ≤ 2 log2(n + 1).

Example: n = 1,000,000 gives height at most about 40, so a lookup needs at most 40 comparisons.

A skip list can be updated with plain CAS operations on single pointers, while rebalancing a tree changes many nodes at once. A rotation touches several parent and child links, which cannot be done atomically without a lock. Inserting into a skip list links one node at each level independently, so a failed CAS just retries.

Result: ConcurrentSkipListMap is lock-free with O(log n) expected time, at the cost of more memory per entry.

It throws NullPointerException, because natural ordering calls compareTo on the key and null has none. Even the first put into an empty TreeMap is checked (since Java 7). A TreeMap built with a custom Comparator that handles null, such as Comparator.nullsFirst(...), can accept a null key. Null values are always allowed.

code.title: PriorityQueue is a heap: array order differs from poll order

followUps:
Mark the old entry as stale and insert a new one with the lower priority (lazy deletion). PriorityQueue has no decrease-key, and remove(Object) is O(n). In Dijkstra, offer (newDist, node) and when polling skip any entry whose distance is larger than the best known.

pq.offer(new int[]{nd, v});
int[] cur = pq.poll();
if (cur[0] > dist[cur[1]]) continue;

The queue may hold up to E entries, so each operation is O(log E).

A 4-ary heap is shallower and touches fewer cache lines, so it can be faster in practice. With 4 children per node the height drops from log2 n to log4 n (half as many levels: 10 instead of 20 for 1,000,000 elements). The four children sit next to each other in the array, usually inside one cache line.

Sift-down compares 4 children per level instead of 2, but memory access dominates, so it often wins for large heaps.

code.title: Fail-fast, weakly consistent and snapshot iterators

followUps:
Use the iterator's own remove(), removeIf, or collect then remove. Iterator.remove updates modCount and the iterator together, so no exception occurs.

Iterator<Integer> it = list.iterator();
while (it.hasNext()) {
    if (it.next() % 2 == 0) it.remove();
}
list.removeIf(x -> x % 2 == 0); // simplest

removeIf on ArrayList is a single O(n) pass, whereas calling list.remove in a loop is O(n2).

Yes, it may; it only promises elements as they existed at some point, not the current state. If the iterator has already passed the bucket nothing changes for it, but if it has not reached an element yet and another thread removes it, the iterator may or may not still return it, depending on timing. The guarantee is that it never throws, never returns the same element twice, and reflects state at or after creation.

Do not rely on it for an exact snapshot; use a copy or a CopyOnWrite structure for that.

code.title: CopyOnWriteArrayList: stable snapshots, costly writes

followUps:
The array field is volatile, so a reader always sees a fully built array published by the last writer. A write builds a new array, then does a volatile write of the reference; a later volatile read of that field gets a happens-before edge to everything stored in the new array. Readers just read the reference once and use that immutable array, so they need no lock.

Elements added are visible to any thread that reads the list after the write completes.

No. subList is a view with a modification check, not a snapshot. It remembers the parent's array and expected state; if the parent changes after the view was created, later calls on the subList throw ConcurrentModificationException. Writes through the view also copy the whole parent array.

Example: sub = cow.subList(0,2); cow.add("x"); sub.size() throws CME. Copy it into a new list if you need a stable slice.

code.title: A key mutated after insertion is lost in a HashMap

followUps:
Take a heap dump and look for a map whose size is larger than what you can look up by key. In a tool like Eclipse MAT, open a HashMap's table, and check whether nodes sit in a bucket that does not match (n-1) & hash for their key's current hashCode, or whether the cached hash field differs from a fresh hashCode().

Symptom first: size() grows while hit rate drops. Prevention: make keys immutable.

Only if every component is itself immutable. A record's hashCode and equals are built from its components, and the fields are final, so the record cannot change; but a component such as a List or an array can be changed from outside, which changes the record's hash.

Example: record Key(List<Integer> ids) is unsafe if someone later calls ids.add(5); use List.copyOf in the constructor.

code.title: Java 7 resize reversed chains (cycle risk); Java 8 keeps order

followUps:
Take a thread dump several times and look for a thread stuck in the same HashMap method. Run jstack <pid> three times a few seconds apart; a thread in HashMap.get or getNode in RUNNABLE state on every dump, with a CPU core at 100%, points to a cyclic chain.

Confirm with the thread's CPU time (top -H matched to the dump's nid in hex). Then fix the data race: use ConcurrentHashMap.

Because a race may need rare timing, so passing runs prove very little. A data race can lose an update only when two threads hit the same bucket within nanoseconds; a test with 4 threads and 1,000 operations may run clean a thousand times and fail in production under 64 cores and a different JIT.

Thread safety must come from the language rules (happens-before, locks, concurrent classes), not from tests. Stress tools like jcstress help but cannot prove absence.

code.title: Memory estimate: boxed HashMap vs primitive open addressing

followUps:
Values from -128 to 127 are cached, so boxing them creates no new object, but a big map mostly holds larger numbers. Long.valueOf(5) returns a shared instance, saving 16 bytes per entry for those values. With 10 million random keys, nearly all values are above 127, so the saving is tiny.

Do not count on the cache for a size estimate unless the data is known to be small, such as counts or flags. Primitive maps avoid the question entirely.

Ten million tiny objects make the heap large and make garbage collection slow. The collector must trace 20 million objects (nodes plus boxed values) every full or old-generation cycle, which means long marking pauses and high CPU. Allocation also floods the young generation while the map fills, and resizing temporarily holds two tables.

Fixes: primitive arrays (one object, nothing to trace), off-heap storage, or a larger heap with a low-pause collector like ZGC.
